result.summary: Homer's verses on feasting are praised as golden, and Hesiod, annoyed, challenges him with riddling half-lines and puzzling questions. Homer answers each, completing Hesiod's verses with apt sense, often drawing on Trojan War and other heroic themes.

scenes.title: Homer's golden verses; Hesiod's challenge
scenes.summary: Homer's praise of feasting is admired by the Greeks. Hesiod, annoyed, poses hard questions and then turns to half-lines of doubtful meaning.
scenes.stakes: Hesiod and Homer compete for poetic reputation; failing to answer would mean losing the contest.

scenes.title: Hesiod's half-lines, Homer's completions
scenes.summary: Hesiod recites unfinished lines and Homer completes each with fitting sense, touching on Heracles, Sarpedon, Argonauts and Agamemnon.
scenes.stakes: Homer must complete each verse aptly or lose the contest.

Homer's witty completion of Hesiod's riddling line.

analysis.text: The contest pits Homer's quick, apt wit against Hesiod's puzzling challenges, showing the poets as rivals in improvisation.
The account reflects later Greek tradition about the two poets' rivalry and the ritual recitation of Homer's lines at feasts.

legacy.text: The Contest of Homer and Hesiod became a famous ancient tale, and Nietzsche wrote about it in his essay Homer's Contest.

fun_facts.text: The Contest of Homer and Hesiod survives in a version from the time of Emperor Hadrian, though it draws on earlier material.

language_notes.text: Libations were offerings of wine poured out to the gods before or during a meal; the verses became a customary formula at public sacrifices.
Felicity here means happy skill in expression, Homer's apt and graceful verse.
Impasse means a blocked position; Homer must answer a riddle-like request that leaves no easy reply.
Homer answers that nothing of the kind will ever happen, since Zeus has no tomb. Hesiod asked for a song of things neither past, present nor future.
Heracles fought giants with his bow, and his arrows were a famous weapon in myth.
Callisto was a nymph of Artemis' band, loved by Zeus; in some versions Artemis killed her.
Sarpedon, a son of Zeus, was a Lycian ally of Troy killed by Patroclus. Homer completes 'Zeus' into 'Zeus-born'.
Colchis and king Aeetes belong to the Argonauts' story: Jason sailed there for the Golden Fleece.

context_notes.text: These lines come from Odysseus' speech to Alcinous in the Odyssey, praising the pleasures of a feast.
This is the Contest of Homer and Hesiod, an ancient tale in which the two poets compete in verse.
The Phrygians were a people of Asia Minor, neighbors of Troy; Homer twists the line into a comic scene.
Agamemnon, king of men, led the Greek army against Troy and was a major leader in the Iliad.

literary_notes.text: Calling the verses golden praises them as the highest quality, and the claim that all guests recite them shows their fame.
Homer ends Hesiod's line with a humorous twist: the Phrygians are skilled at ships, yet are made to steal dinner.
Homer's quick completion shows his wit and skill at turning a half-line into a neat, sensible maxim.
Hesiod's line turns a host's welcome into a curse, leaving a sinister sense for Homer to repair.
